Every screen has things pushing in from: The status bar, the home indicator, the keyboard, and your own headers and tab bars.
Harbor gives each one a place, so your content stops doing inset arithmetic.
It starts with the sea. Mount it once, above your navigator, and every harbor floats on it.
The coast is what the platform takes: the status bar, the home indicator, a notch.
On a television, the coast is the title-safe band around the edge of the screen.
The pier, built out over the water.
A header your content scrolls under.
Boats pass beneath the pier, the way your rows slide under the header.
The quay, a stone wall on the shore.
A tab bar your content stops at.
The tug pulls up to the quay wall, and the list comes to rest right above the tab bar.
Where a boat passes under the pier, the water ripples: that is the wake.
Rows fade as they slide under the header, then rest past the fade.
A moored boat is tied clear of everything in its way.
A form or a fixed button keeps clear of the docks, the coast and the keyboard.
The mooring line is the page margin, kept by the rows that ask for it.
The list runs to the edge of the screen, so a carousel inside it can too.
The fairway is the channel boats sail through.
It is a scroll view that runs under the docks and comes to rest clear of them.
A header inside the list pins at the face of the docks, and the next one stacks below it.
A sticky pill rides with its row, then holds below the docks until the row scrolls away.
Open water ignores the docks: a background, a map, a hero image.
It runs under the header, edge to edge, as the sea runs under a pier.
The tide is the keyboard.
When it comes in, a dock on pilings stays where it is, and the water covers it. That's your tab bar.
A floating dock rides up with the tide. That's your composer, sitting right on top of the keyboard.
A dry dock keeps the keyboard's ground, tide in or out, so nothing moves when it comes and goes.
Content can ask a dock to make way: to go dark, or to withdraw and give back its ground.
A pontoon is a dock moored from deep inside the page, like an unsaved changes bar.
A buoy floats in the clear water: a floating button, a speech bubble by its anchor.
A modal buoy puts a barrier over the page. Tap beside it, or go back, and it closes.
A portal buoy opens from anywhere: a menu from a list row flips above it when there is no room.
A signal is a toast. It goes to the page on top, clear of the docks, and screen readers announce it.
A sheet is a new port of its own, with its own pier and its own floating quay.
It stops short of the status bar, and its footer clears the home indicator once.
A breakwater sheet tells the page how much of it is covered, so the page keeps clear of it.
A dialog can keep to the clear water of the page that opened it.
The lighthouse keeps things in sight: a focused field is brought back above the keyboard.
On a television, a scale model lays the harbor out on a reference screen and scales it to fit.
The chart shows every dock's ground, each harbor's clear water, and the tide, as you work.
Sea trials test it all on real devices: phones, foldables and televisions, with the keyboard up.
Docks claim the edges. Everything else moors clear of them.
